finding.claim: Unauthenticated remote code execution via Marshal.load of attacker-supplied data
finding.source: params[:state] from POST /restore (form field, query string, or multipart body). Reachable by any network client; no authentication.

trace.note: post "/restore" route accepts any unauthenticated request
params[:state] is read and base64-decoded with no length, format, or signature check

Marshal.load deserializes the bytes, instantiating arbitrary Ruby objects and running their marshal/_load hooks; attacker-chosen object graphs can reach dangerous methods via known gadget chains in Ruby core and common gems
The resulting object is .inspect'd, so the return value also reflects the attacker's object graph

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization on the route (app.rb:5). No HMAC or signature on the state blob. Marshal has no safe-load mode. No input size limit or class allowlist. Rack::Protection (Sinatra default) does not inspect body contents or prevent deserialization. No control in this code stops exploitation short of network-level restrictions.

verdict.guard_found: none. The route at app.rb:5 has no auth, and line 6 calls Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(params[:state])) with no signature, size, or class check. The only other file in the directory is app.rb, so no middleware or config adds a guard.
verdict.reason: Any anonymous client can POST attacker-controlled bytes to /restore, and app.rb:6 passes them straight to Marshal.load, so the insecure-deserialization sink is reachable with no effective control. The source and sink match the candidate's trace. Full RCE is not shown by this code alone: it depends on gadget chains available in the runtime's loaded classes, which the candidate describes only in general terms.

finding.claim: Reflected HTML injection in /import response (possible cross-origin XSS if Sinatra origin protection is disabled)
finding.source: Attacker-chosen top-level JSON object keys in the raw request body read at app.rb:11 (request.body.read).
finding.sink: Response body data.keys.join(",") at app.rb:12, returned with Sinatra's default text/html Content-Type and no HTML escaping.

trace.note: Raw body is read and parsed as JSON; request.body.read ignores Content-Type, so a text/plain form-encoded body can carry the same JSON
Keys containing markup are joined and returned verbatim
Browser renders the response as HTML in this app's origin

finding.guards_checked: Sinatra default Rack::Protection (protection true) includes HttpOrigin, which likely rejects cross-origin POSTs with a mismatched Origin, so third-party form submission is probably blocked by default. Not verified against the actual Sinatra version or whether protection is disabled. No output escaping or explicit text/plain Content-Type is set. Direct attackers gain nothing extra since they can already POST here.

verdict.guard_found: Sinatra's default Rack::Protection (on by default for classic Sinatra apps; app.rb does not set `protection` to false). Its HttpOrigin check, which is in the default set and which I did not verify in the installed version, rejects cross-site browser POSTs whose Origin header does not match the host. A cross-site form POST to /import carries the attacker's Origin, so it should be rejected before app.rb:11-12 runs. No output escaping or explicit text/plain Content-Type exists at app.rb:12.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (app.rb:11 reads the raw body and app.rb:12 joins the keys unescaped into a text/html response), but a cross-origin browser POST to /import should be blocked by Sinatra's default HttpOrigin protection, which the app does not disable, so the attacker cannot reach the sink. The verdict depends on that default being active in the Sinatra version in use, which the repo (no Gemfile) does not show.
